LOWELL BEGINNING NORTH TURN | IMPACTS ON THE WAY FOR HAWAII🌀🌧️🌊Hurricane Lowell remains a powerful Category 4 Hurricane with sustained winds of 145 mph and gusts of 175 mph. Lowell looks to pass roughly 100-200 miles west of Kauai County Monday night, likely near Major-Hurricane strength.

Conditions will begin deteriorating Sunday afternoon and evening as deep tropical moisture spreads across the islands. Periods of heavy rain and thunderstorms may continue through Tuesday morning - and potentially into Wednesday - with flash flooding and mudslides possible statewide. Rainfall totals of 3-6 inches are forecast for Kauai and the Big Island, with localized amounts exceeding 10 inches possible. Strong southeast-to-south winds will also develop, especially across Kauai County, where tropical-storm conditions are possible late Monday or Monday night.

Dangerous surf will rapidly build along south-and west-facing shores, potentially becoming very large and destructive Monday. Combined with monthly high tides, coastal flooding could affect roads, properties, harbors and channels. Even though Lowell’s center is forecast to remain west of the main islands, impacts will extend hundreds of miles from the hurricane. Small track changes could significantly alter the severity of conditions, especially around Kauai🌀

SOCAL COASTAL FLOODING & HIGH SURF THIS WEEKEND🌊🌀a Coastal Flood Advisory and High Surf Advisory are in effect today through Tuesday for much of the Southern California coast as a large southerly swell generated by Hurricane Marie arrives during a period of high astronomical tides. It should be noted that Marie will NOT make landfall in Southern California but will still be powerful enough to generate the coastal flood and surf concerns.

From Ventura and Los Angeles Counties south through Orange and San Diego Counties, large waves, dangerous rip currents, beach erosion and periods of minor to moderate coastal flooding will be possible. The greatest impacts will favor south and southwest-facing beaches and other vulnerable low-lying coastal locations.

🌊 Los Angeles-Ventura: Breaking waves of 5–8 feet are expected. Coastal flooding could become most noticeable around the evening high tides - roughly 5PM this evening, 6PM Sunday, 7PM Monday and 8PM Tuesday. Low-lying beaches, walkways and parking lots could briefly flood, with Avalon, the Alamitos Peninsula, Malibu and Point Mugu among the more vulnerable locations

🌊 Orange-San Diego Counties: Surf could reach 6-10 feet on south-southwest-facing beaches and 4-7 feet along west-facing beaches, with strong rip and longshore currents and localized coastal flooding possible

HURRICANE MARIE MOISTURE HEADING INTO THE WEST🌀🌧️Hurricane Marie will remain well offshore of California, but its tropical moisture will still influence parts of the West this weekend, with another potentially broader surge possible next week.

The first push of moisture is already being drawn northeast ahead of a West Coast trough. Southern California will see increasing rain chances through Sunday, with generally light rainfall but locally heavier amounts around the mountains and foothills. A few thunderstorms are possible, and heavier showers could produce localized flooding.

By Sunday, the moisture plume stretches farther northeast across the Mojave Desert, southern Nevada, northwest Arizona and Utah. Rain and thunderstorms will become more scattered farther east, but pockets of heavier rainfall will be possible, particularly from the Mojave Desert into southern Nevada and southwest Utah. Then attention turns to next week.

Marie is forecast to gradually weaken and turn more northwest to northward while remaining hundreds of miles offshore. Another Pacific trough could eventually capture some of Marie’s remnant tropical moisture and pull it northward along the West Coast and into the Great Basin during the middle to latter part of next week.

That could bring another increase in showers and thunderstorms across portions of California and Nevada, with some of that moisture potentially reaching Oregon and even the Pacific Northwest later in the week. Exactly how far north and inland the moisture gets remains uncertain and will depend heavily on the position of the next trough.

So again, while Marie is not forecast to make landfall in California, it's tropical moisture will get pulled away from the Hurricane in multiple waves. The first arrives this weekend, followed by the potential for a second and possibly broader surge next week. This does not mean it will rain everywhere or every day, but the overall pattern continues to favor periods of unusually deep moisture across portions of the West🌀🌧️

MORE STORMS POSSIBLE ACROSS THE NORTHWEST TODAY BUT COVERAGE LOOKS LESS THAN FRIDAY⛈️another round of showers and isolated thunderstorms is expected across portions of Washington, Oregon and Idaho this afternoon and evening as a cool upper-level low continues spinning over the Pacific Northwest. The Storm Prediction Center does have the entire region in a chance for thunderstorms but don't let that fool you, not everyone sees storms and most folks won't see storms.

If the atmosphere can recover from yesterday's storms, parts of Western Washington could be fairly active again this afternoon. Thunderstorms are expected to initially develop around the Cascades before some drift west toward the Puget Sound lowlands, similar to what happened Friday but, again, there are questions on how much destabilization occrus. Not everyone will see a storm, but lightning, locally heavy rain and gusty outflow winds will be possible underneath the stronger cells. Activity should gradually decrease around sunset.

Across northwest Oregon and southwest Washington, scattered showers will redevelop with daytime heating, particularly around the Cascades and Coast Range. A few stronger, pulse-type thunderstorms could develop, capable of brief heavy rain, small hail, lightning and gusty-erratic winds.

Central and eastern Washington into northeast Oregon will also see scattered showers and a few thunderstorms. The Washington Cascades and northern Blue Mountains appear to have some of the better chances, although isolated activity is possible elsewhere. Instability is relatively weak, so widespread severe weather is not expected.

Around Bend and central Oregon, showers will remain possible as disturbances rotate around the upper low, with isolated thunderstorms mainly favoring the higher terrain. The overall setup continues to favor hit-or-miss rather than widespread storms. Southern Oregon will be quieter than yesterday with the best chances around the southern Oregon Cascades into northern Klamath County. Farther east, most of southwest Idaho should also be considerably drier today with only very isolated storms, mainly around eastern Valley County, Idaho, and western Baker County, Oregon.

If storms approach, move indoors and be especially careful if you're hiking or camping in the mountains. This is where storm coverage will be higher and lightning is likely⛈️

WIDESPREAD DAMAGING WINDS THIS AFTERNOON⚠️⛈️💨the severe weather risk is increasing this afternoon across parts of Virginia and the Carolinas, with the greatest concern across central and eastern North Carolina. The atmosphere is becoming very unstable, with thunderstorms strengthening and organizing as they move east. items.author: NTXWC
items.text:
The STRONGEST El Niño EVER recorded is upon us, which will have SERIOUS effects on how our weather pattern plays out this winter.

An El Niño pattern happens when sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean become warmer than average.

This year, they are forecast to be the strongest we have *ever* seen. 

Strong El Niño winters typically feature a stronger, more active southern storm track, increasing the odds of wetter and sometimes cooler conditions across the southern U.S. 

That can mean more frequent storm systems crossing Texas and, when cold air is available, opportunities for winter storms, ice and snow. It does NOT guarantee a snowy winter, but an active subtropical jet gives us more systems capable of producing precipitation when cold air happens to be in place. 

A more active storm track means more storm energy for severe weather outbreaks as well. One unforgettable analog is the 2015-16 super El Niño. On December 26, 2015, North Texas experienced a major tornado outbreak producing 12 tornadoes, including the deadly Garland-Rowlett EF4. The outbreak killed 13 people. The 2015-16 El Niño was among the strongest on record.

Does this mean we will see widespread tornado outbreaks on the daily? Absolutely not. But going into an even stronger pattern than we've ever seen is certainly ringing alarm bells for a potentially anomalous winter across the southeast. 

Again, a strong El Niño does NOT mean tornadoes will strike your house, or a historic winter storm will dump buckets of snow on the southeast. There is no way to predict individual events. 

Think of it as potential energy storing up. This pattern will give us more storm track energy and opportunities to see frequent cold swings and severe weather outbreaks, but there is no saying in how, when, or where these specific events will play out. Only time will tell if the strongest El Niño will really live up to it's name.

items.text:
COULD OKLAHOMA SEE ABOVE-NORMAL SNOWFALL THIS WINTER?

I’ve been digging through Tulsa’s snowfall history and comparing it with past El Niño winters, and there are some interesting numbers that have my attention as we look ahead to this winter.

First, Tulsa’s current 30-year normal seasonal snowfall is about 8.7 inches.

When you look back through the historical record, several El Niño winters have produced some very impressive snowfall totals in Tulsa.

1957–58: 17.2 inches
1963–64: 13.9 inches
1969–70: 20.4 inches
1972–73: 14.1 inches
1987–88: 18.2 inches
2002–03: 20.4 inches
2006–07: around 15 inches
2009–10: 22.8 inches

Those aren’t small departures from normal. Several of those winters produced roughly double Tulsa’s normal seasonal snowfall, and 2009–10 ended up being one of the snowiest winter seasons in Tulsa’s historical record.

Now, does El Niño automatically mean Oklahoma gets buried in snow?

No. And that’s important.

We’ve also had El Niño winters with very little snow. The 1997–98 winter produced only about 3.4 inches in Tulsa, and the most recent El Niño winter, 2023–24, produced only about 1.6 inches.

But El Niño can change the overall setup in a way that becomes favorable for Oklahoma.

During many El Niño winters, the southern storm track becomes more active. That can mean more systems moving across the southern United States and potentially more opportunities for precipitation across Oklahoma.

And that’s really what I’m interested in.

More opportunities.

To get a snowy winter in Oklahoma, you need storms. Then you need enough cold air available when those storms arrive.

If we can get those two ingredients to overlap several times this winter, snowfall can add up quickly.

A storm arriving with temperatures in the upper 30s gives us a cold rain.

Move that same storm into Oklahoma with temperatures below freezing and suddenly we’re talking about snow, sleet or freezing rain.

That’s why seasonal snowfall forecasting is so difficult here. The difference between a winter with 4 inches and one with 20 inches can come down to the timing of cold air with just a handful of storms.

Still, when I put the historical data together with the larger pattern we’re watching, I’m leaning toward Oklahoma having a better opportunity for above-normal snowfall this winter.

That’s not a prediction that Tulsa will receive 15 or 20 inches of snow. We’re simply too far away to responsibly make a snowfall forecast that specific.

But if you’re asking which direction I would lean right now?

I would lean snowier than normal rather than less snowy than normal.

There are enough pieces on the table to make this winter particularly interesting.

And remember, Oklahoma doesn’t need four straight months of bitter cold to have a big snow season. Sometimes all it takes is a few well-timed storms with cold air already established.

We’ve seen that happen before.

So for the snow lovers who have been waiting for another active Oklahoma winter, I wouldn’t start buying the sleds just yet…

But I also wouldn’t put them too far back in the garage.

Using the 4-Factor FeelsLike 
Forecast, most cities will peak between 108-114°F.
4 Factors: Temp + Humidity + Sun + Wind. Believe it or not, traditional NOAA heat index forecasts do NOT include the sun and wind. I’ve always thought they should because many folks spend so much time exposed, especially on weekends. So, I found a formula from Dr. Robert Steadman in an old research paper - a version of which is being used by the Australian Bureau of Meteorology right now. Sun spikes it. In sunny spots the sun adds up to 15°. Generally wind cools it. In Florida this time of year there’s lots of sun, but minimal wind so these numbers are 5-10° higher than NOAA’s heat index (in the shade). Bottom line: you can NOT directly compare this to our NOAA traditional heat index, and it should not be used to replace it. It does illustrate how being in the Sun makes a dramatic difference. So… shade is your friend this weekend. Be safe!! #Florida #heat @topfans

HURRICANE MARIE MOISTURE SURGES INTO SW🌧️🌴⚠️Hurricane Marie will remain well offshore, but a plume of its tropical moisture will get pulled north and northeast across parts of the Southwest this Labor Day Weekend. Rain chances begin increasing Saturday, but Sunday looks like the main day for widespread showers, thunderstorms and locally heavy rain from Southern California northeast through the Mojave Desert, southern Nevada, northwestern Arizona and Utah.

Southern California will see increasing tropical moisture Saturday into Sunday. Around Los Angeles, Sunday currently has the greatest rain potential, with most locations expected to receive less than 0.50" and many under 0.25", although locally higher totals are possible in the mountains or beneath heavier showers. San Diego and surrounding areas have a lower overall rainfall signal, but scattered showers remain possible, especially Sunday.

Farther northeast, the moisture plume becomes more impressive. Across southern Nevada, southeastern California and northwestern Arizona, a band of rain is expected to develop Sunday. Current projections generally favor 0.250.50", but locally heavier amounts will be possible depending on exactly where the rain band sets up. Northern Arizona will also see increasing moisture, with Sunday bringing the greatest rain and thunderstorm coverage, especially across northwestern Arizona and near the Grand Canyon.

Utah may end up beneath one of the more favorable setups for heavier rainfall. Tropical moisture interacting with a strong upper-level disturbance should produce widespread, quick-moving showers and thunderstorms Sunday. The Weather Prediction Center has placed a corridor from near Las Vegas and the Grand Canyon northeastward through portions of Utah in the best chance to see excessive rainfall and some flooding, including areas around Zion and Bryce Canyon. Slot canyons, normally dry washes, burn scars and other flood-prone terrain could become particularly dangerous if heavier rain develops.

This does not mean everyone will see heavy rain or that it will rain throughout the entire holiday weekend. Saturday looks more scattered, while Sunday currently has the strongest signal for a broader surge of tropical moisture and locally heavy rainfall. Where heavier showers or thunderstorms develop, localized flash flooding will be possible, especially across the deserts, mountains and slot-canyon country🌧️🌴⚠️

MONITORING MARIE | 2 ROUNDS OF MOISTURE🌧️🌴Hurricane Marie is expected to remain well offshore of California, but its tropical moisture could influence parts of the West in multiple waves over the next week! The first push arrives this weekend as moisture from Marie is pulled northward ahead of a trough along the West Coast. Southern California should see increasing clouds and shower chances Saturday into Sunday, with Sunday looking like the wetter day. A few thunderstorms will also be possible, especially across the mountains and deserts. This deeper moisture will spread into southeast California and southern Nevada, into Utah and northern Arizona, bringing an increase in showers and thunderstorms there as well. Farther north across the Great Basin and interior Northwest, additional rain is expected into early next week, although not all of that moisture can necessarily be directly attributed to Marie.

Then attention turns to a possible second push of tropical moisture during the middle to latter part of next week. Forecast confidence is much lower with this round, but there continues to be a signal for another trough to develop over the Eastern Pacific while Marie weakens well offshore. That pattern could potentially draw additional remnant tropical moisture northward into California and portions of the West.

Importantly, this does not mean Marie is forecast to hit California. The circulation itself should remain well offshore and weaken. The story is the moisture being pulled away from the system and transported northward. Exactly how much moisture reaches the West - and where it goes - will depend heavily on the evolution of Marie and the Pacific trough, so the mid-to-late week portion of the forecast remains something to monitor🌧️🌴

MORE THUNDERSTORMS ACROSS THE NORTHWEST TODAY⛈️a cold upper-level storm system remains over the Pacific Northwest, keeping temperatures unusually cool while creating enough instability for another round of showers and thunderstorms. Across western Washington, showers and isolated thunderstorms will redevelop, particularly near the Cascades, with some activity potentially drifting toward the lowlands. Western Oregon will see increasing thunderstorm chances late this morning and afternoon, especially south of Portland and around the Coast Range and Cascades. Some of the better thunderstorm coverage will extend across southern and central Oregon, including around Bend, before spreading into eastern Oregon and southwest Idaho. Scattered thunderstorms are also possible across eastern Washington, northern Idaho and portions of western Montana.

Severe weather is not the main concern, but stronger cells could produce brief heavy rain, small hail, frequent lightning and locally gusty winds. Storm movement may be slow in some areas, allowing localized heavier rainfall. Given the cold upper low, steep low-level lapse rates and weakly sheared-showery environment, a low-end cold-air funnel is possible, particularly across western Washington and Oregon. Most funnels in this type of environment are brief and remain harmless, although a very small percentage can occasionally reach the ground. Overall, the greatest thunderstorm coverage today should favor Oregon into southwest Idaho⛈️

items.text: Hurricane Hunters are specialized military and civilian aircrews who fly directly into tropical cyclones to gather critical, real-time weather data. Operating highly instrumented aircrafts, they deploy sensors like dropsondes into the eye of the storm to measure wind speed, air pressure, temperature, and humidity from the inside out. This extreme, hands-on data collection provides the precise information needed to build accurate forecasting models, predict a storm's path and intensity, and issue life-saving evacuation warnings.

items.author: ericsnitilwx
items.text:
ARE WE SEEING MORE TORNADOES? It's a reasonable question to ask. The state of New York is now up to 20 confirmed tornadoes this year. On average (based on 2006-2025 data), New York sees about 9 tornadoes per year. So, we've already doubled that figure in 2026. 

Also heavily biasing our recent memory is what took place in 2024 when we shattered records with 32 confirmed tornadoes. Looking at data dating back to the 1950s, there is most certainly a trendline toward increasing tornado counts in time (smoothing out the inherent variability for individual years) in New York.

The bigger question is, why? That's a more complex answer. The answer is certainly not limited to the idea that we're simply having more tornadoes forming in New York than we did in the past. Technology has improved dramatically. Boots on the ground with eyes on storms has increased dramatically. Video & photo evidence (everyone has a smartphone in their pocket) has increased dramatically. Put another way, our ability to DETECT & CONFIRM tornadoes plays a role in the increasing numbers. 

So, are we having more tornadoes? Probably. The numbers are certainly going up with time. But perhaps the better way of putting that is we're "confirming" more tornadoes that otherwise might have been missed many years ago. As our climate continues to change, what's considered "normal" will continue to evolve. This, alongside continued improvements in technology, will make it very difficult for apples to apples comparisons to the past.

items.author: powponder
items.text:
No Signs of Fall…

This Summer doesn’t have an off button. I know it was disappointing that Southeast Texas received 27” of rain and North Texas got little to nothing. Yesterday’s “cooler day” still managed a high of 94 with 102 heat index. Average highs are 92 right now now and drop into the 80s starting next Sunday. 

Mother Nature has other plans this year and Texas doesn’t do “normal” weather very well. The dreaded ridge is coming back and it’s massive for September. Rain free and triple digits return. Not record territory for Labor Day weekend, but records start coming down late next week to 101 range and that’s doable to break. Lows near 80
and highs in the low 100s are the dog days of Summer weather. The extended dry streak continues for the foreseeable future. 

The light at the end of the tunnel would be to get one of these Pacific storms to turn North and get caught up in the jet stream to slingshot into Texas. We need something big to disrupt this weather pattern and I’m not seeing it until Fall actually gets here. 
#Summer #September

MAJOR CATEGORY 4 HURRICANE LOWELL⚠️Major Hurricane Lowell bears watching closely through the Labor Day weekend if you're a resident of or visiting Hawaii! Lowell remains a Category 4 Hurricane with sustained winds of 130 mph, and gusts of 160 mph, located about 495 miles south-southwest of Hilo tonight. The Hurricane is moving west but is forecast to slow before making a sharp turn toward the northwest and north this weekend.

That turn will be critical. Lowell could move near the western Hawaiian Islands late Sunday through Monday night, potentially still as a Major Hurricane, but confidence remains low on exactly how close the center will come to the Islands, and impacts could range from minor to major depending on where and when that northward turn occurs. A positive note is that there has been a slight westward jog in guidance which would keep Lowell a little farther away from Hawaii.

Even without a direct hit, however, of Hawaii could experience dangerous surf, coastal flooding-storm surge, strong winds and heavy rainfall, with the greatest concern currently toward the western end of the State, particularly Kauai County. Coastal inundation could also be worsened by peak monthly high tides Monday. Swells from Lowell will produce increasingly dangerous, potentially life-threatening surf and rip currents over the next several days.

There are no coastal watches or warnings in effect at this time but everyone in Hawaii should closely monitor Lowell through the weekend and have Hurricane plans and supplies ready. The forecast should become clearer as the Hurricane approaches its expected turn north⚠️

MONITORING MARIE🌧️🌴Hurricane Marie is expected to remain well offshore of California, but its tropical moisture could influence parts of the state and other parts of the West in multiple waves over the next week.

The first push arrives this weekend, with tropical moisture increasing across Southern California late Saturday into Sunday. Sunday currently looks like the wetter day, with showers and a few thunderstorms possible, including for coastal areas and valleys and mountains-coastal slopes. Moisture will spread inland as well, increasing shower and thunderstorm chances across the deserts and parts of Nevada, and other parts of the West.

Then attention turns to mid-to-late next week. Over the past day, there has been a noticeable trend in some guidance toward eventually turning Marie or its weakening circulation northward over the eastern Pacific. This is not currently the official forecast and remains highly uncertain, but it is worth watching. Marie would be weakening and remain well offshore, but a northward turn could help pull its remnant tropical moisture into California mid week and beyond. Higher confidence in the evolution of Marie will develop over the coming days🌧️🌴

items.author: DylanFedericoWx
items.text: HURRICANE THREAT - Hawaii needs to be on alert as Hurricane Lowell approaches from the southwest next week. Early indications are Lowell passes uncomfortably close to the west of Kauai next Tuesday. However, we’re talking 6 days out — and a lot can change that far out. What I do know is, Lowell will be a large and mature hurricane by that time, so major impacts especially heavy flooding rain will be felt far away from the center even if the core misses west. However, a direct major hurricane strike similar to Iniki in 1992 is on the table, so forecast trends must be closely monitored in the coming days. Stay tuned.

SOCAL COASTAL FLOODING & HIGH SURF THIS WEEKEND🌊 a Coastal Flood Advisory and High Surf Advisory are in effect Saturday through Tuesday for much of the Southern California coast as a large southerly swell generated by Hurricane Marie arrives during a period of high astronomical tides. It should be noted that Marie will NOT make landfall in Southern California but will still be powerful enough to generate the coastal flood and surf concerns.

From Ventura and Los Angeles Counties south through Orange and San Diego Counties, large waves, dangerous rip currents, beach erosion and periods of minor to moderate coastal flooding will be possible. The greatest impacts will favor south and southwest-facing beaches and other vulnerable low-lying coastal locations.

🌊 Los Angeles-Ventura: Breaking waves of 5–8 feet are expected. Coastal flooding could become most noticeable around the evening high tides - roughly 5PM Saturday, 6PM Sunday, 7PM Monday and 8PM Tuesday. Low-lying beaches, walkways and parking lots could briefly flood, with Avalon, the Alamitos Peninsula, Malibu and Point Mugu among the more vulnerable locations

🌊 Orange-San Diego Counties: Surf could reach 6-10 feet on south-southwest-facing beaches and 4-7 feet along west-facing beaches, with strong rip and longshore currents and localized coastal flooding possible

items.author: MeteorologistChristopherNunley
items.text: HIT-OR-MISS STORMS POSSIBLE ACROSS THE NORTHWEST FRIDAY⛈️a cool upper-level storm will remain over the Northwest Friday, keeping the atmosphere unstable enough for scattered showers and thunderstorms. The better thunderstorm potential stretches from western and southern Oregon into southeast Oregon, central Idaho, southeast Washington and the Idaho Panhandle. Some areas could see a few rounds of showers, with storms capable of brief heavy rain, small hail, lightning and gusty-erratic winds. With unusually cold air aloft, and the favorable placement of the low, there will also be a VERY LOW-end chance for a brief cold-air funnel or possibly landspout, particularly beneath stronger showers or thunderstorms across Oregon. This is a low probability, localized threat. Thunderstorm chances look lower across western Washington and much of western Montana, where showers will be more common than storms. This is not expected to be a widespread severe weather event, but locally heavy rain could create flooding concerns, especially across parts of Oregon and Idaho where rainfall has already been substantial⛈️
